question: Where can I find a fractional CRO?
body:
## Direct Answer

You can find a fractional CRO through specialized fractional-executive marketplaces (Bolster, Go Fractional, Continuum), boutique firms that place seasoned revenue leaders (Chief Outsiders, SBI Growth), operator communities like Pavilion, and warm referrals from your investors, board, and RevOps network. The right channel depends on whether you want a vetted match fast, a firm-backed engagement with bench support, or a peer-sourced introduction you can reference-check yourself.

A fractional Chief Revenue Officer is a senior revenue leader who works with your company part-time — often one to three days a week — to build the go-to-market engine, fix the funnel, coach the sales team, and install the operating rhythm a full-time CRO would, but at a fraction of the cost and commitment. The hard part is rarely the concept; it's the sourcing. Below is a practical map of where these people actually live, how each channel is different, what to screen for, and how to run the engagement once you've found the right person so you don't burn three months discovering a mismatch.

## What exactly is a fractional CRO and when do you need one?

A fractional CRO owns the *revenue* function — not just sales. That means they sit above sales, marketing alignment, RevOps, partnerships, and often customer success, and they're accountable for the number and the system that produces it. Unlike a consultant who delivers a report and leaves, a fractional CRO embeds: they run your pipeline reviews, sit in your forecast calls, rebuild your comp plan, and hold reps accountable. Unlike a full-time CRO, they do this across two to four companies at once, which is exactly why the model works for a business that needs senior revenue leadership but can't yet justify — or afford — a $300K-plus base plus equity hire.

The clearest signals you need one: you're a founder still personally closing every deal and it doesn't scale; you've hired reps but have no repeatable playbook, so performance is random; your forecast is a guess and the board no longer believes it; or you're between full-time revenue leaders and can't let the engine coast for six months. Fractional is the wrong answer when you genuinely need a full-time butt-in-seat leader for a large team, when the problem is a single broken system that a focused RevOps engagement would fix more cheaply, or when what you actually want is a closer rather than a leader. Getting this diagnosis right *before* you start sourcing saves you from interviewing the wrong archetype entirely. If you're unsure which gap you're filling, our breakdown of [the revenue leadership ladder](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/cro-vs-vp-sales) walks through where a CRO's mandate starts and a VP of Sales' ends.

![Where can I find a fractional CRO — figure 1](/assets/qa/tl9001-b1.jpg)


It helps to understand why this role even exists as a market. Over the last several years, two things converged: a generation of experienced revenue executives decided they'd rather advise several companies than own one org chart, and a wave of capital-efficient startups discovered they needed senior GTM judgment long before they could carry a senior GTM salary. The fractional model sits precisely in that gap. It is not a discount version of a real CRO and it is not a glorified advisor — at its best it is the same caliber of operator you'd fight to hire full-time, deliberately structured so that a company at the wrong stage for a permanent hire can still access that judgment. Recognizing this framing changes how you source: you are not looking for someone cheap and available, you are looking for someone senior who has chosen this model on purpose and treats their portfolio like a craft. The candidates who drifted into fractional work only because they couldn't land a full-time seat are a different, weaker pool, and your sourcing channel largely determines which pool you're fishing in.

## Where do you actually find a fractional CRO?

There are five distinct channels, and each optimizes for something different — speed, vetting depth, firm backing, price, or trust. The best sourcing strategy runs two or three in parallel rather than betting on one.

![Where can I find a fractional CRO — figure 2](/assets/qa/tl9001-b2.jpg)


**Fractional-executive marketplaces** are the fastest structured path. Platforms like **Bolster**, **Go Fractional**, **Continuum**, and **Toptal** maintain vetted rosters of fractional and interim executives and match you against your stage, industry, and motion. You post a role or brief, they surface candidates, and you interview a shortlist within days. The trade-off is that match quality depends on the platform's vetting bar, and you're often paying a marketplace margin on top of the executive's rate. **Boutique fractional-executive firms** — **Chief Outsiders**, **SBI Growth**, **Fractional Officer** — go deeper: they place a partner-level leader *and* back them with a bench, methodology, and firm accountability, which lowers your key-person risk but raises the price and can feel less like "your" executive. **Operator communities** like **Pavilion** and **RevGenius** are where a huge number of fractional CROs actually hang out; posting in the right channel or asking the community team for intros surfaces people who are actively taking fractional work and come pre-referenced by peers. **Your own network** — investors, board members, other founders, and RevOps leaders — is the highest-trust channel because every candidate arrives with a built-in reference. And **LinkedIn plus content-driven inbound** works if you're patient: many strong fractional CROs are semi-public, posting about GTM, and reachable directly.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[You need a fractional CRO] --> B{What matters most}
  B -->|Speed and structure| C[Marketplaces]
  B -->|Firm backing and method| D[Boutique firms]
  B -->|Peer trust and fit| E[Operator communities]
  B -->|Highest trust| F[Warm network referrals]
  C --> G[Shortlist in days]
  D --> H[Partner plus bench]
  E --> I[Pre referenced operators]
  F --> J[Built in references]
  G --> K[Reference check and pilot]
  H --> K
  I --> K
  J --> K
  K --> L[Signed engagement]

![Where can I find a fractional CRO — figure 3](/assets/qa/tl9001-b3.jpg)

```

The diagram above collapses to one lesson: no matter which channel surfaces the person, every path should funnel into the same reference-check-and-pilot gate before you sign. The channel gets you a name; the gate protects you from a bad hire.

Whichever channels you run, the quality of what comes back is downstream of the quality of your brief. A weak request — "we need help with sales" — attracts generalists and forces every candidate to guess at your problem. A sharp brief does the filtering for you before a single interview happens. Name your stage and revenue band, your motion (product-led versus sales-led, self-serve versus enterprise, inbound versus outbound), your average deal size and sales cycle, the specific breakage you feel (forecast you don't trust, reps who won't ramp, a leaky funnel), the three outcomes you'd call success, and the days-per-week and term you have budget for. Post that same brief into a marketplace, a Pavilion channel, and a note to three investors on the same afternoon, and within a week you'll have a comparably-shaped shortlist from three independent sources — which is exactly what you want, because a candidate who surfaces in two channels at once has effectively been referenced twice. Resist the urge to widen the brief to attract more people; a narrower brief that repels the wrong candidates is doing its job.

## How much does a fractional CRO cost and how are engagements structured?

Fractional CRO compensation is structured in a few recognizable shapes, and understanding the shape matters more than chasing a single headline number — because the same person will quote very differently depending on days per week, engagement length, and whether equity is involved. The three common structures are a **monthly retainer** tied to a fixed number of days per week, a **day rate** for more variable or project-shaped work, and a **cash-plus-equity** blend that's common at early-stage startups where the company wants to conserve cash and align the leader to outcomes. Retainers dominate because both sides want predictability: the CRO can plan their portfolio, and you can budget.

Rates vary enormously by market, seniority, and the size of the revenue problem, so treat any figure you see online as a starting anchor rather than a quote — an ex-CRO of a public company commands a different rate than a first-time fractional leader, and a two-day-a-week embedded engagement costs far more than a monthly advisory cadence. What you're really pricing is *leverage*: a strong fractional CRO should pay for themselves by tightening conversion, improving forecast accuracy, and preventing bad hires, not by being cheap. When you evaluate cost, compare it against the fully-loaded cost of a full-time CRO (base, bonus, equity, benefits, and the ramp risk) and against the cost of *not* fixing the revenue engine for another two quarters. For a deeper model of how to think about the revenue math of a senior GTM hire, see our [RevOps cost-of-delay framework](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revops-cost-of-delay). Always get the structure — days, term, notice period, scope, and success criteria — in writing before you start.

Beyond the headline structure, a few practical terms decide whether the arrangement stays healthy. Clarify the **billing cadence and payment terms** up front — most fractional leaders invoice monthly in advance for a retainer, which is normal and signals they run their practice like a business. Watch for **scope creep in both directions**: a leader carrying too many clients may quietly shrink your days, while an intense rebuild phase may need more days than the steady-state number you budgeted, so build a mechanism to flex up or down by mutual agreement rather than renegotiating from scratch. If equity is on the table, treat it like any other grant — a real vesting schedule and cliff, not a handshake — and make sure the cash portion still covers the leader's baseline so they're not effectively subsidizing you. Finally, price in the *ramp*: even a strong fractional CRO spends the first few weeks learning your data, deals, and people, so don't judge the engagement on week two. The right frame is total value over the term against the fully-loaded alternative, not the invoice in isolation.

## How do you vet and choose the right fractional CRO?

Vetting a fractional CRO is different from vetting a full-timer because you have less time to course-correct and the person is dividing attention across clients. Your screen should be sharper and faster. Start with **pattern-match on motion, not logo**: a CRO who scaled a product-led, low-ACV SaaS motion may be the wrong fit for your enterprise, six-figure, multi-stakeholder deals, no matter how impressive the résumé. Ask what the company looked like *when they arrived* and *when they left*, and what specifically they changed — comp, territory design, forecast method, hiring bar. Vague answers ("I aligned the team") are a red flag; specific answers ("I moved us from a rep-led to a manager-led forecast and cut slippage by rebuilding stage exit criteria") are the signal.

Then run three checks in parallel. First, **references you source yourself**, not just the ones they hand you — a founder they worked for, a rep they managed, and ideally a board member. Second, a **paid pilot or a working session**: give them a real slice of your pipeline or a real forecast call and watch how they think, because you learn more in one live pipeline review than in three interviews. Third, **capacity and conflict**: ask exactly how many clients they carry, whether any are competitive with you, and how they protect your days when a client fire flares up. The best fractional CROs are transparent about their portfolio and disciplined about boundaries. Finally, screen for the soft skill that decides everything at the fractional level — the ability to influence and drive change *without* the positional authority of a full-time exec. If they can't get your team to adopt a new operating rhythm as a part-timer, the engagement fails regardless of pedigree.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Candidate] --> B[Motion match]
  B --> C[Self sourced references]
  C --> D[Paid pilot session]
  D --> E[Capacity and conflict check]
  E --> F{Clear on all four}
  F -->|Yes| G[Sign engagement]
  F -->|No| H[Pass and keep sourcing]
```

Treat the four gates as a sequence, not a menu. A candidate who nails the motion match but stumbles on the pilot has told you something real about how they operate under your specific conditions — believe the pilot over the pedigree.

A short bank of pointed questions makes the interview do real work. Ask "Walk me through the last forecast you rebuilt — what did it look like before, what did you change, and what did the board see three months later?" to test for systems thinking over anecdotes. Ask "What's a change you drove that the team initially resisted, and how did you get adoption?" to test the influence-without-authority muscle directly. Ask "Tell me about a fractional engagement that didn't work — what went wrong and whose fault was it?" — a candidate who can name their own contribution to a failure is far safer than one whose every story ends in triumph. And ask "How do you decide which client gets your attention on a Tuesday when two of them have a crisis?" to hear how they actually manage a portfolio. You're listening for specifics, self-awareness, and a repeatable method, not charisma. The most dangerous hire is the one who interviews brilliantly and has never once said the words "here's what I got wrong."

## How do you set up the engagement so it actually works?

Finding the person is half the job; the other half is designing the engagement so a part-time leader can produce full-time-quality outcomes. The single biggest failure mode is a fuzzy mandate. Before day one, write down the **top three outcomes** you're buying — for example, a rebuilt and believable forecast, a documented sales playbook, and a hiring scorecard for your next two reps — and the **rhythm** the CRO will own (weekly pipeline review, monthly forecast, quarterly business review). Ambiguity is expensive at one to three days a week because every hour spent re-negotiating scope is an hour not spent fixing revenue.

Give them real authority and real access. A fractional CRO who can't see your CRM data, can't sit in deal reviews, or can't influence comp is being set up to fail. Grant system access on day one, announce the mandate to the team so the CRO isn't seen as an outside consultant, and be explicit with your reps about who the CRO can direct. Establish a **direct line to you** (the founder or CEO) on a fixed cadence so blockers surface fast. Plan for **knowledge transfer from the start** — the goal of most fractional engagements is to build a system and a team that eventually runs without the fractional leader, or to bridge to a full-time hire the fractional CRO helps you recruit. Define what "graduation" looks like: either the internal team owns the rhythm, or you've hired the permanent leader. To keep the engagement measurable, agree on a small set of leading indicators — forecast accuracy, stage conversion, ramp time — and review them monthly. Our guide to [the RevOps operating cadence](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revops-operating-cadence) lays out the review rhythm that keeps a part-time leader accountable to full-time results.

It helps to think in a rough 30-60-90 arc so both sides know what "on track" looks like. In the **first 30 days**, the CRO is diagnosing, not overhauling: pulling data, sitting in on live deals, interviewing reps, and coming back to you with a written read on what's actually broken versus what you assumed was broken. Resist the urge to demand quick wins here — a leader who reorganizes the team in week two before understanding it is a warning sign, not a hero. By **day 60**, you should see the first structural changes land: a rebuilt forecast method, revised stage definitions, an early cut of the playbook, or a fixed comp wrinkle — concrete artifacts, not slideware. By **day 90**, the operating rhythm should be running under its own weight, the leading indicators should be trending, and you should be able to point to specific decisions that went differently because the CRO was in the room. If you reach day 90 and can't name what changed, that's your signal to have a direct conversation — the value of a fractional leader is that the engagement is cheap to correct or end compared to a full-time miscast, so use that optionality rather than letting a soft engagement drift into a fourth quarter.

## Related questions

### What's the difference between a fractional CRO and a sales consultant?
A consultant diagnoses and advises, then leaves; a fractional CRO embeds part-time and *owns* the revenue number, runs the operating rhythm, manages the team, and is accountable for outcomes — not just recommendations.

### How many hours a week does a fractional CRO work?
Most engagements run one to three days per week, though it varies by company size and urgency. Early, intensive rebuilds skew higher; steady-state advisory-plus-oversight engagements skew lower and may flex month to month.

### Can a startup afford a fractional CRO?
Usually yes — that's the point of the model. You get senior revenue leadership at a fraction of a full-time CRO's fully-loaded cost, often via retainer or cash-plus-equity, making it accessible well before you can justify the full-time hire.

### Should I hire a fractional CRO or a full-time VP of Sales?
Hire the fractional CRO when you need to *design and install* the revenue system and don't yet have a repeatable motion; hire the full-time VP when you have a proven playbook and need someone to run and scale a growing team day to day.

### How long do fractional CRO engagements last?
Commonly a few months to a couple of years. Many are designed to bridge to a full-time hire or to graduate once the internal team owns the operating rhythm, with a defined notice period so either side can adjust.

## FAQ

**What does a fractional CRO actually do?**
They own the revenue engine part-time: building the go-to-market playbook, fixing the funnel, rebuilding forecasting and comp, coaching sales leadership, aligning marketing and RevOps, and installing the operating cadence — while remaining accountable to the number, not just delivering advice.

**Where is the fastest place to find a fractional CRO?**
Fractional-executive marketplaces like Bolster, Go Fractional, and Continuum are the fastest structured route — you can interview a vetted shortlist within days. For higher trust, ask your investors, board, and operator communities like Pavilion for warm referrals in parallel.

**How do I know if a fractional CRO is legitimate and good?**
Screen for motion match over logos, source your own references (a founder, a rep, and a board member), run a paid pilot on real pipeline, and confirm their client load and any competitive conflicts. Specific, measurable past changes beat vague claims of "alignment."

**Do fractional CROs take equity?**
Sometimes. At early-stage startups a cash-plus-equity blend is common because it conserves cash and aligns the leader to outcomes. More established companies typically use a straight monthly retainer or day rate. Structure depends on stage, cash position, and engagement length.

**Can a fractional CRO manage my sales team?**
Yes, if you grant real authority and access. They can run pipeline reviews, coach and hold reps accountable, and direct the team — but only if you announce the mandate, give CRM and deal-review access, and make clear to the team who the CRO can direct.

**How is a fractional CRO different from an interim CRO?**
A fractional CRO works part-time, usually across multiple companies, as an ongoing arrangement. An interim CRO is typically full-time but temporary — a stopgap filling a vacancy until a permanent leader is hired. Some professionals and firms offer both.

**What should be in a fractional CRO engagement agreement?**
Days per week, engagement term and notice period, the top three outcomes you're buying, the operating rhythm they own, system access, decision authority, success metrics, confidentiality, and any conflict-of-interest disclosure about competing clients.

**When should I NOT hire a fractional CRO?**
When you need a full-time leader for a large, established team; when the real problem is a single broken system a focused RevOps engagement would fix more cheaply; or when what you actually want is a closer rather than a revenue leader who builds systems.

**How do I write a brief that attracts the right candidates?**
Name your stage and revenue band, your motion and average deal size, the specific breakage you feel, the three outcomes that would count as success, and the days-per-week and term you can fund. A narrow brief that repels the wrong people is doing its job.

**What does a good first 90 days look like?**
Diagnosis in the first 30 days, the first structural changes landing by day 60, and a self-sustaining operating rhythm with trending indicators by day 90. If you can't name what changed by day 90, treat it as a signal to correct or end the engagement.
